newsitem.title: USA: Fed says no intervention in forex mart in Q4 '96.
newsitem.headline: Fed says no intervention in forex mart in Q4 '96.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York said U.S. monetary authorities did not intervene in the foreign exchange markets in the fourth quarter of 1996, setting a new record for the longest period of abstinence since Fed record keeping began in 1977.
"I believe it is the longest time since perhaps the Smithsonian Accord," said New York Fed executive vice president Peter Fisher at a press conference on Wednesday.
The Smithsonian Agreement, passed in 1971, was a watershed pact by the Group of 10 industrial nations over specific exchange rate adjustments as well as a devaluation of the U.S. dollar against gold.
U.S. monetary authorities have not intervened in the currency market, buying or selling dollars for foreign currencies, since they purchased dollars on August 15, 1995, Fisher said.
The 16-1/2 month dearth of intervention as of December 1996 surpassed the previous record -- a 14-1/2 month dry spell from March 30, 1981 to June 14, 1982, he said.
When asked whether intervention was ever seriously discussed in the last quarter by monetary officials, Fisher declined to comment.

In the quarter, the dollar appreciated in a relatively orderly manner, rising 3.9 percent against the yen, 0.9 percent versus the mark, and 0.2 percent on a trade-weighted basis against other G-10 currencies, the Fed said in a report presented to Congress.
"The relative stability that characterized foreign exchange markets through the first three quarters of 1996 continued during the period," the report said.

"Although the average daily trading range for the dollar increased slightly from the previous quarter, it remained substantially less than the range observed for the same period in 1995," the report added.
On average, the dollar traded in a daily range of 0.7 percent against both the mark and the yen in the quarter.
This compares with daily ranges of 0.6 percent against both currencies in the previous period and with 1.0 percent against the mark and 1.1 percent against the yen for the fourth quarter of 1995.

The sharpest one-day move was an almost two-yen fall in the dollar on November 7 following remarks from Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, suggesting that Japan's economic weakness was overstated and that the yen was unlikely to weaken further.
Fisher said Sakakibara was "trying to keep the markets boring" by slowing the dollar's rapid ascent against the yen.

The dollar strengthened in the period despite a shift in market expectation from anticipation of a near-term tightening of U.S. monetary policy to the view that the Federal Open Market Committee would not take any action through the end of the year.
Bolstering the U.S. unit were perceptions of substantial Japanese capital outflows and calls from several European officials welcoming further depreciation of their currencies, the report said.
Also, general optimism regarding the prospects for European Economic and Monetary Union prompted flows out of marks into other European currencies.
"The dollar appreciated during the period as non-U.S. factors appeared to dominate currency trading," the report said.
International trade data seemingly had little impact on foreign exchange trading.

At the end of the quarter, foreign currency reserve holdings of the Federal Reserve System and the U.S. Treasury Department's Exchange Stabilization Fund were valued at $19.2 billion and $15.6 billion, respectively, and consisted of marks and yen.
